name: Parsol 1789 (avobenzone)

lead: Avobenzone, often labelled Parsol 1789, is the main UVA-absorbing filter in chemical sunscreens. It is used at up to 3 percent in the US and 5 percent in the EU.
It breaks down in sunlight unless stabilized, so formulators pair it with other filters such as octocrylene.

paras: It absorbs UVA light around 357-360 nm and dissipates the energy, mostly as heat.

Clinical trials found it enters the bloodstream after application, with unknown clinical significance. The FDA has said more safety data are needed for GRASE status. Palau has banned it over reef concerns.

lead: Avobenzone, sold under trade names including Parsol 1789, Eusolex 9020 and Escalol 517, is an oil-soluble organic filter used in sunscreens to absorb ultraviolet A (UVA) light, with peak absorption near 357 to 360 nm.[1] It is a dibenzoylmethane derivative with the formula C20H22O3.[1]

It is among the most widely used UVA filters. In the United States it is permitted at up to 3 percent in over-the-counter sunscreens, and in the EU at up to 5 percent.[1] A known property is its photoinstability: it can lose absorbance under sunlight, so formulators pair it with stabilizers such as octocrylene.[1][2]

Two randomized clinical trials published in JAMA found that avobenzone and other tested active ingredients entered the bloodstream after sunscreen application; the studies did not assess whether this causes harm.[3][4]

paras: Avobenzone (4-tert-butyl-4'-methoxydibenzoylmethane) is a pale crystalline solid that does not dissolve in water but dissolves in oils and common cosmetic emollients.[1][5] It exists mainly as an enol form stabilized by hydrogen bonding, and this enol form absorbs UVA strongly.[1][5] Industrial synthesis uses a Claisen condensation.[1]

Wikipedia reports that a day of temperate-climate UVA exposure can degrade most of the filter in a product, and cites industry data showing a 36 percent drop in absorbance after an hour of sun.[1] Reviews of UV filter chemistry discuss methods to stabilize it in formulations.[6]

Stabilization strategies in the literature include combining it with octocrylene, with the triazine filter Tinosorb S, or with antioxidants.[1][7][8] Wikipedia adds that uncoated mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide can accelerate its breakdown.[1]

According to Wikipedia, avobenzone was patented in 1973, approved in the EU in 1978 and approved by the US FDA in 1988.[1] In 2021 the FDA said avobenzone did not meet its definition of generally recognized as safe and effective pending further safety data, though it remains the only FDA-approved UVA organic filter.[1] It is also approved in Australia and Japan.[1] Palau banned it in 2020 over reef-toxicity concerns.[1]

The FDA asks that sunscreen ingredients with systemic absorption above 0.5 ng/mL undergo additional toxicology assessment.[3] In a 2019 randomized trial of four commercial sunscreens applied under maximal-use conditions, avobenzone and the other tested actives were detected in plasma at levels above that threshold.[3] A 2020 follow-up trial of six active ingredients, including avobenzone, reported similar results and that concentrations rose above the threshold quickly after application.[4] The authors stated that these findings do not indicate people should avoid sunscreen, and that clinical significance had not been established.
A 2017 study reported that chlorinated water and UV light can break avobenzone into other compounds, including phenols and aldehydes.[1] The compound can also stain clothing a yellow-orange color.[1]

Avobenzone is one of several organic filters detected in aquatic environments. A 2021 systematic review and ecological risk assessment examined organic UV filters in aquatic settings,[9] and a field study at French Mediterranean beaches estimated UV filter input from bathers.[10]

Two randomized trials in JAMA (2019 and 2020) measured plasma concentrations of avobenzone and other actives after sunscreen application and found systemic absorption above the FDA's 0.5 ng/mL threshold.[3][4] They were pharmacokinetic studies and did not assess skin cancer, photoaging or other clinical outcomes. In vitro work has compared the photostability of filter combinations and broad-spectrum protection.[7][11]

timeline.event: JAMA maximal-use trial detects systemic absorption of avobenzone and other filters.[3]
Second JAMA trial confirms absorption above the 0.5 ng/mL threshold; Palau bans avobenzone.[4][1]
FDA states avobenzone lacks sufficient data for GRASE status.[1]
